Maladaptive Strategies.value: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Fire/flame cues are hard to reconcile with a childhood domestic-violence witnessing trauma profile when the rest of the trigger, memory, threat, and appraisal items do not suggest fire, arson, or burn-related trauma content. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
issues.explanation: 'No longer capable of doing the things that defined me' suggests a loss of prior adult identity/functioning that is difficult to fit with a 19-year-old whose index trauma was childhood witnessed domestic violence. The other appraisals center on helplessness and failed protection, which fit better; this item is comparatively implausible for the developmental context.

vignette:
Maria is a nineteen-year-old train conductor who grew up in a small apartment in the Bronx, where she often heard her father’s fists against her mother’s body and the screaming that followed. The most vivid sound was a particular crash—a heavy lamp falling—that left a metallic, bitter taste in her mouth, and now, years later, when the memory surfaces, she can still taste it, and the event feels as though it is happening all over again, though she can never put the moments in the right order. At work, a sudden blast of a train horn or the roar of a passing freight will yank her back into that apartment; the noise itself triggers the memory so powerfully that she sometimes flinches in the conductor’s booth, her heart hammering, and that pounding in her chest then becomes yet another trigger, a somatic signal that she is about to be overwhelmed. Her heart racing also makes her feel utterly helpless—she cannot stop bad things from happening—and she immediately blames herself: if only she had screamed louder, or hidden in a different way, the event would not have unfolded as it did. These negative appraisals feed back into the memory, making it feel more urgent and more present, because she is certain she should have protected her mother and failed.

To cope, Maria keeps impossibly busy. After every shift she volunteers to work overtime, cleans her apartment obsessively, and spends hours replaying “what if” scenarios—imagining how life would have been different if the event had never happened, which paradoxically loops her right back into the memory, making it feel even more current. She also restricts her eating, skipping breakfast and lunch most days, telling herself that food feels heavy and unnecessary, but the undereating sometimes makes her heart race from low blood sugar, and that racing heart is itself a trigger, drawing her into another cycle of intrusions and self-blame.

Nighttime is the hardest. As a train conductor, she often works late shifts that end after midnight, and she has to walk through dark train yards and empty platforms. She finds it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, so she checks and rechecks every door and lock in her small apartment before she can even consider sleeping. On those nights when the sense of threat pressed in hardest, the memory of the lamp falling would surface unbidden — vivid and immediate, as if the darkness itself had pulled it from her. The darkness feels alive to her, and she stays on high alert, listening for any unexpected sound—a creak, a distant shout—and each sound threatens to bring the past flooding back. Her hypervigilance also deepens her sense of helplessness: she is convinced she cannot protect herself or anyone else, and this belief makes the memory more fragmented and more intrusive.

The threat she feels does not stay contained; it spills into her daily life. When she checks the locks, she is also monitoring her own body, waiting for her heart to pound, and her hardened vigilance makes her more attuned to loud noises, so a dropped toolbox in the yard becomes a trigger, and her mind jumps to that metallic taste again. In turn, her continued caution reinforces her negative appraisals—she must have done something wrong to end up this scared—and she doubles down on her maladaptive strategies, working even harder to stay busy so that she does not have to sit with the fear, and skipping meals because eating feels like a vulnerability she cannot afford.

The cost has been concrete. Maria was recently written up at work for missing a signal check during a night run; her supervisor noted she seemed “distracted and jumpy.” She began to realize she could not keep going this way. What frightened her most was the thought that if she stopped keeping busy, the memory would swallow her whole. But she also began to hope, quietly, that maybe there was a way to live without tasting the past every time a train thundered past. That is why she finally walked into the clinic—to see if someone could help her find a way out of the loop she cannot escape on her own. That memory had taught her that if she could rehearse every possible alternative, maybe she could find a version where she felt less guilty—and so the replaying became a compulsive ritual she could not stop, even though it only deepened her distress.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not directly convey that the sense of threat causes or influences the trauma memory; it only shows that threat leads to hypervigilance which amplifies response to triggers that then trigger memory, but no direct causal link from threat to memory is stated.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not directly convey that the sense of threat causes or influences the trauma memory; it only shows that threat leads to hypervigilance which amplifies response to triggers that then trigger memory, but no direct causal link from threat to memory is stated.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
